title: Pardons Robert Zangrillo
description_short: Trump granted a presidential pardon to Robert Zangrillo as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: Trump granted Robert Zangrillo a presidential pardon on May 24, 2018. The Justice Department’s clemency list identifies the District of Massachusetts and lists counts involving mail and wire fraud, honest-services fraud, federal-program bribery, and money laundering. The list gives no sentence or case disposition, and it does not state why Trump granted the pardon.
description_long: Trump granted Robert Zangrillo a presidential pardon on May 24, 2018. The Justice Department’s clemency list places the case in the District of Massachusetts and names conspiracy involving mail and wire fraud, honest-services fraud, federal-program bribery, and money laundering, along with related counts. It lists no sentence or final case disposition. The allegations concern financial and public-integrity offenses, but the listing alone does not show whether the case had ended in a conviction, whether charges remained pending, or what conduct Zangrillo admitted or contested. That distinction affects what the pardon resolved and its practical legal effect. The clemency record also provides no explanation from Trump or his administration for selecting Zangrillo. Without the case outcome and the terms or rationale accompanying the pardon, the event can be described as a grant of clemency in a case involving those listed offenses, but not as a judgment on guilt or proof of a political connection.

title: Pardons Abel Holtz
description_short: Trump granted a presidential pardon to Abel Holtz as part of a clemency list.

The Justice Department lists a Southern District of Florida conviction for obstruction of justice, with 45 days’ imprisonment, two years of supervised release, and a $20,000 fine. The entry notes that the sentence was amended. The available record does not provide the president’s rationale for granting clemency.
description_long: Trump pardoned Abel Holtz on January 19, 2021, near the end of his first term. The Justice Department lists Holtz’s case in the Southern District of Florida and identifies obstruction of justice as the offense. It records a 45-day prison term, two years of supervised release with conditions, and a $20,000 fine; the sentence had been amended. The pardon followed a conviction and sentence that included incarceration, supervision, and a financial penalty. The clemency list does not describe the arguments made in support of Holtz or explain why Trump granted relief. It also does not specify how the pardon affected any remaining conditions or financial obligations. The record establishes the pardon and the sentence associated with the conviction, but not a political connection or rationale for the decision. Holtz’s case was one of several clemency actions announced on January 19, 2021, Trump’s final full day in office.

The Justice Department lists Cooper’s convictions in the Western District of North Carolina for conspiring to possess marijuana with intent to distribute, conspiring to commit money laundering, and structuring currency transactions. title: Appeals Court Rejects Immunity Claim in Election Case
description_short: The D.C. Circuit rejected Trump’s claim of presidential immunity in the federal election interference case.
description_medium: On February 6, 2024, a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit rejected Trump’s claim that presidential immunity barred the federal election-interference prosecution. The ruling addressed whether the case could proceed, not whether Trump was guilty of the charged conduct. Trump could continue seeking Supreme Court review, so the decision did not itself resolve the criminal case.
description_long: On February 6, 2024, a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit rejected Trump’s claim that absolute presidential immunity barred his federal election-interference prosecution. The panel concluded that former presidents do not have categorical immunity from criminal prosecution for conduct alleged to be unofficial. Its decision allowed the case to proceed at that stage, while leaving the underlying charges for the criminal process. Trump could seek further review, so the ruling did not end the litigation or decide whether he committed the charged offenses. The appeal turned on whether a former president could avoid prosecution for alleged efforts to overturn the 2020 election by invoking his former office. The decision affected the case’s timing and legal path, but it was not a trial verdict. The charged conduct and the immunity question remained separate issues for later proceedings.
organization_tags: U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit

title: Trump Asks Supreme Court to Overturn Colorado Ballot Ruling
description_short: Trump petitioned the Supreme Court to reverse Colorado’s decision removing him from the primary ballot.
description_medium: On January 3, 2024, Trump asked the U.S. Supreme Court to overturn Colorado’s decision excluding him from the state’s presidential primary ballot. The Colorado Supreme Court had relied on Section 3 of the Fourteenth Amendment, concerning participation in insurrection. Trump remained on the ballot while the appeal was pending; his petition asked the justices to review the dispute but did not decide it.
description_long: Trump petitioned the U.S. Supreme Court on January 3, 2024, asking it to reverse Colorado’s ruling that he could not appear on the state’s presidential primary ballot. The Colorado Supreme Court had applied Section 3 of the Fourteenth Amendment, which bars certain people who engaged in insurrection from holding federal office. The state case asked whether the provision applied to Trump and whether his conduct surrounding January 6, 2021, made him ineligible. The petition brought those questions before the nation’s highest court and raised disputes about the amendment’s scope and its enforcement in presidential elections. Trump remained on the Colorado ballot while Supreme Court review was pending. His filing sought a decision; it did not resolve the constitutional issue or establish the merits of the underlying allegations. The dispute put a state ballot ruling and a federal constitutional question on a compressed election timetable.
organization_tags: Supreme Court of the United States
